1:
The chapter is dated only by its relation to the last. John Gill explains that this was not literally the second time the word came, since it had come many more times, but the second time on the same occasion and subject. Matthew Henry draws a lesson from the repetition: God speaks once, yea twice, for the encouragement of his people, since we are not only so disobedient that we need precept upon precept but so distrustful that we need promise upon promise. He makes more of the place. This word, like the last, came while the prophet was in prison; no confinement can deprive God’s people of his presence, and no locks can shut out his gracious visits—often as their afflictions abound their consolations abound more, and they have the most reviving communications of his favour when the world frowns; the Apostle’s sweetest letters, Henry notes, bore date out of a prison. John Calvin gives two reasons for the repetition. It was necessary to render the Jews inexcusable, since they pretended ignorance unless God repeated himself—the principle on which the Apostle said everything should be established by two or three witnesses. But God had also a care for the faithful, that they might not faint under trials lasting so long: some would die in exile and might forget the covenant, and those who were to return needed no common support to keep them firm for seventy years. Calvin notes the prophet’s own position, that he was bidden to consult the benefit of enemies who had clamorously condemned him and now left him lying in prison. Adam Clarke dates the chapter to the eleventh year of Zedekiah and places the prophet in the court of the prison, where the elders and the king’s officers could consult him more easily; they kept inquiring, he says, foolishly imagining that if he would prophesy good things these must come.

Clarke also gives the chapter’s plan: a restoration attended by circumstances that shall astonish the world, a description of the prosperity that follows, and the promise of the Messiah and of the stability the people shall enjoy—promises which, so far as they respect the great body of the Jews, he holds still to be fulfilled.

The titles in the second verse ground everything that follows. Keil and Delitzsch resolve the pronouns from the sense: the Lord does what he says and forms what he wants to make in order to accomplish it. They gloss the second verb as framing in the mind, as if to think out, and the third as realising what has been determined. Calvin builds the chapter’s argument on the same titles: God is the maker and former of Jerusalem, so there is no doubt he will rescue it from the hands of enemies, and raise it even from hell itself. He weighs whether the verbs are past or present, allowing either—that God built the city at first, or that he purposes to create it anew—and draws out the first. Nothing under the sun is perpetual, and the fashion of this world passes away, so that changes take place in all cities; but God by a singular privilege exempted this one from the common lot, and its ruin therefore could not be perpetual. Henry infers more briefly that he who built Jerusalem at first can rebuild it, and built it for his own praise and therefore will. Clarke prefers the doer of it to the maker thereof, citing a translator who renders the clause as the Lord who does what he has said, and insists the divine name should be used in all such places. Gill reports the referents proposed for the pronoun—the prophet, the earth, Jerusalem, or the promise itself—and admits the last if the church is understood; John Wesley takes it of Jerusalem or of the promises, God having a sufficiency in himself to make good his word.
3:
The invitation in the third verse is understood as directed to the prophet himself. John Gill says it is spoken not to Jerusalem and its inhabitants but to him, encouraging him to seek the Lord with the promise of an answer. Adam Clarke makes the contrast with the diviners: to God alone belongs the revealing of what is future, so that while the idolaters go to their gods for information about the present commotions and find no light in them, the prophet is told to ask and be told the great things even he does not know. John Calvin insists it was said not so much for the prophet’s sake as for others’. He had no doubt prayed earnestly, and his prison must have inflamed his ardour, so God is not reproving his sloth; the word is directed to him so as to excite all the godly to pray. There is an implied reproof, as though it were their own fault that God did not cheer them with a joyful message, since they had closed the door against themselves, bolting up their hearts with unbelief. Calvin draws the lesson: whenever we are worn out by affliction it is our own fault, because we are slow to pray, for everyone who cries acknowledges that God is near, as the psalm promises to those who truly call on him; if long grief brings no comfort, that happens through our neglect. He notes that the last words cannot be rendered quite literally.

The houses named in the fourth verse are read as the occasion of the whole prophecy. Charles Ellicott takes them to point to the incident that prompted it: the houses had been destroyed either by the invaders or, more probably, by the besieged themselves, to raise a counter-work against the enemy’s mounds; and the word rendered swords, translated axes elsewhere, includes tools for breaking down walls. Calvin canvasses two constructions. Some say the houses were pulled down for the sake of the warlike engines, that these might be made from the materials; but the sense is more obvious, he thinks, if the houses were thrown down by the engines and by the sword. He notes that the word for the engines is rendered fortifications by some, but when the storming of cities is spoken of it must mean machines for throwing darts or battering rams, though we do not know their form. He also observes that the kings of Judah were not satisfied with one palace but had many houses outside the city. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as houses broken down because of the besiegers’ mounds and because of the sword. Gill takes the destruction now being fulfilled as a pledge of the blessings promised afterwards, assuring the prophet that as he would see the one fulfilled, so certainly would the other come to pass; Clarke states the same double message, that the city shall fall and the rest be carried away, but the nation shall be preserved and return.

The fifth verse describes a sortie and its outcome. Ellicott notes that the construction is participial, with the force of an indefinite they, and that the prophet sees a sally of the besieged doomed to failure, so that the houses are filled with those slain by the sword as well as by famine and pestilence. Calvin makes the same reading a rebuke of false confidence. The participle sets before their eyes what was to be, as though the prophet said they will rush forth boldly and think themselves equal or superior to the Chaldeans—said in order to ridicule their audacity, the sad issue following at once in the filling of their own houses with corpses. He proposes joining the two verses, which he thinks have been improperly separated, so that the participle stands with the sword rather than alone, and gives a rendering accordingly.
6:
The promise turns on a medical figure, and the commentators press it in different directions. Charles Ellicott identifies the first word, as elsewhere in the book, as the bandage or plaster which was prominent in the therapeutics of the East, and suggests that both words may have been spoken in direct contrast with the pestilence then ravaging the city; in any case, he says, they carry a higher and figurative meaning, since it was true of the city and its people that the whole head was sick and the whole heart faint, and God promises to manifest himself as the healer of a spiritual disease worse than any pestilence. Adam Clarke gives the same word its homely sense of an extensive plaster, one as large as the sore, and takes the promise literally as repairing the losses of families by numerous births and blessing the land with fertility. John Wesley keeps the figure at the level of the nation, whose miserable disturbed state is compared to wounds and sickness, so that its restoration to a peaceable and prosperous condition is fitly called its health and cure. John Gill takes it wholly of the church and of spiritual maladies, the diseases of sin healed through the blood of the Messiah who should arise with healing in his wings, that is, with the remission of sin which is often meant by healing in Scripture.

John Calvin calls this the main point of the passage. He had been showing until now that the Jews deserved so heavy a punishment because their obstinacy never ceased provoking God; here he promises to be propitious to them after moderate correction, the design of the whole prophecy being to sustain them so that they might not despond but rely on the promise of favour however bitter the exile. He explains the word rendered health from a root meaning lengthening, that is, of a man’s life, and so taken in the sense of recovery. On the second noun he reports and rejects an alternative. Some render it prayer, since the verb behind it can mean both to pray and to multiply, and on that reading God would be promising an access to prayer—a thing worth promising, since matters were so hopeless that no one dared utter a word, and the prophet himself had been forbidden to pray, God having resolved to destroy men of whose repentance there was no hope. But Calvin thinks this explanation too far-fetched and takes the simpler sense, that God would give them abundance of peace, or rather its prolonging and continuance; and peace, as is well known, means a happy state.

The seventh verse names both kingdoms, and that raises a question of date. Clarke says it must respect the later times, since the ten tribes did not return with the Jews at the end of the seventy years. Gill argues the same way and draws a further conclusion: the mention of Israel as well as Judah shows that the prophecy does not relate to the return from Babylon at all, and is to be understood spiritually of the release of the mystical Israel from the captivity of sin and the law by the Messiah. The promise of building them as at the first, which follows, is read by all as the guarantee that the restoration will not be a diminished thing but a return to the original state.
8:
Two verbs of forgiveness stand together, and John Calvin asks why. He says the prophet no doubt repeats the same thing, but the words are not superfluous: it was necessary to remind the Jews seriously of their many vices, of which they were conscious and yet did not repent; since they perversely followed their own wills, the prophet had to goad them sharply, so that they might know they were exposed to eternal destruction if God’s mercy—and that by no means a common mercy—did not come to their aid. He therefore represents the greatness of their sins in order to extol the greatness of the pardon. Calvin also corrects a natural misreading of the first verb. One might understand cleansing to mean regeneration, and this seems probable to those not well acquainted with the language of Scripture, but the word properly means to expiate; it refers therefore not to regeneration but to forgiveness, so that the two clauses say the same thing twice. He explains why so many words are spent on it: hypocrites always extenuate the heinousness of their guilt, and the favour of God would never have been appreciated by the Jews had the atrocity of their sins not been clearly made known to them; the change from singular to plural in the nouns, he adds, shows the mass and variety of their offences, the heaps of evils being so multiplied that they could not be counted. Keil and Delitzsch put the same point structurally: the prosperity just promised gains stability and permanence through the people being cleansed by forgiveness, which elsewhere in the book forms the basis of the new covenant. John Gill refers the cleansing to the blood of Christ which cleanses from all sin of heart, lip and life, in allusion to the purifications under the law, and Adam Clarke holds that these promises of pardon and holiness must be referred to the people’s state under the gospel, when they shall have received the promised Messiah.

The ninth verse describes the effect on those looking on. Keil and Delitzsch explain the phrase carefully: the word means a name rather than fame, and since a name in Scripture always expresses the essential nature, the meaning is that Jerusalem will develop into a city over which men rejoice whenever her name is mentioned. They gloss the following pair as meaning a subject of praise and of glory among all nations, and take the trembling of those who hear not as fear in the ordinary sense but as the effect of being seized with awe at proofs of the wonderful power of God set against the helplessness of their own idols. Charles Ellicott distinguishes two aspects in the bearing of this on the outlying nations: on the one hand they shall sing the praises of the restored city, on the other they shall fear and tremble before its greatness, as showing that it stood under the protection of the Lord of Israel. The word for fear, he notes, is used elsewhere for the quivering, trembling emotion that accompanies great joy, and is perhaps used here to convey that the fear would not be a mere slavish terror. John Wesley reads it more narrowly still, as a fear to engage against a nation so beloved and favoured. Clarke reads the same clause practically: the surrounding nations shall be persuaded that it is the hand of the Almighty that has wrought this change, and shall fear to molest the people and tremble lest they incur the displeasure of their God by doing them any evil. Gill takes the whole verse of the church and people of God, redeemed and rebuilt and cleansed and forgiven, who become a cause of joy to themselves and to others and bring praise and honour to God.
10:
The promise is now given a local address. Charles Ellicott notes that it is repeated with a more local distinctness: this place is probably Jerusalem, and the streets are more strictly the open places, the bazaars or even the outskirts, which were deserted during the progress of the siege and were now waste and silent, but which would in time re-echo with sounds of jubilant exultation. Keil and Delitzsch take the same phrase as specified by the cities named beside it, and read the following verse as a promise that in a land now emptied of men and beasts shepherds with their flocks shall again move about and lie down. John Calvin holds that these two verses have been improperly divided, since the sentence is not complete at the break and what is to be heard is only stated afterwards. He explains the fullness of the passage by the difficulty of believing it: it was hard to muster courage under so great a calamity, and even after a breathing time new trials might have cast them down; the memory of the favour would not have stayed fixed without repeated confirmation, and God is introduced as speaker so that the promise might have more effect. He also hears a reproach in the way the desolation is described. The Jews put every obstacle in the way of their own restoration, for the narrowness of our hearts shuts out God’s favour, and swollen with unbelief we do not let his grace enter; by imagining their calamity incurable they rejected, so far as in them lay, the promised deliverance. What they said was true enough as a matter of fact, Calvin allows—the country and the cities were destroyed and neither man nor beast remained—but the ungodly do not feel the scourges as they should.

Matthew Henry takes the passage as a further prediction of the happy state of Judah after the return, issuing at length in the kingdom of the Messiah. Everyone concluded that the country would lie desolate for ever, with no beasts in the land and no inhabitant in the streets and therefore nothing but perpetual melancholy; but though weeping may endure for a time, joy will return. It had been threatened earlier in the book that the voice of joy and gladness should cease there, and here it is promised that they shall revive. Henry divides the joy in two. There shall be common joy—marriages again celebrated as formerly with songs, which in exile they had laid aside, their harps being hung on the willow-trees; and there shall be religious joy, the temple-songs revived, the Lord’s songs which they could not sing in a strange land, heard now in private houses and in the cities as well as in the temple. Nothing, he adds, is more the praise and honour of a people than that God should have the glory of their restoration, the glory both of the power and of the goodness by which it is effected.

John Gill reads the voice of joy of the gospel, glad tidings to all who see their lost estate, containing peace and pardon through the blood of Christ and rest in him; it is a voice of joy to believers, who hear in it of the one they love, and since they are continually sinning the doctrine of pardon must be joyful to them. Adam Clarke takes the voice of those who say praise the Lord of hosts for the voice of the Levites in the sacred service, intimating that the temple should be rebuilt and the public worship restored. Gill notes at the outset that the tenth verse connects with the beginning of what follows and that the intervening description is a parenthesis.
12:
The picture of the restored land is drawn from pasturage, and John Calvin explains why that image was chosen. He is speaking of the settled happiness of the people, so that the Israelites need not fear that God will fail to open them a way of return and to protect them afterwards; and in setting out their quiet condition he speaks of shepherds, since it is a sure sign of peace when flocks and herds are led into the fields in security. Enemies always gape after prey, as the experience of wars proves: whenever an incursion is made, spies are sent to learn whether there are any shepherds or keepers of cattle, and by that they know whether there is a prey for them. Since shepherds dare not go out when an invasion is feared, and there is then no liberty, the prophet marks the tranquillity of the coming state by putting the shepherds back in the fields. Calvin anticipates an objection from a reader not much acquainted with Scripture, that the promise would then be confined to shepherds and herdsmen; the answer, he says, is obvious—the promise is general but expressed in this way, that God would be the guardian of his people, so that shepherds would drive their flocks here and there in perfect safety and without fear of danger. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse the same way, that in a land now laid waste and emptied of men and beasts, shepherds with their flocks shall again move about and lie down. Adam Clarke refers the reader to a parallel earlier in the book, and John Gill observes that the formula opening the verse is often repeated to give authority to what is said and to command belief. John Wesley glosses the description of the place as meaning that a great part of it is already desolate and the other part soon will be.

The thirteenth verse fills in the map. The regions named—the cities of the hill country, the cities of the lowland, the cities of the south, the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem and the cities of Judah—are taken by the commentators as covering the whole territory, so that no part of it is left out of the promise. Keil and Delitzsch note the phrase describing the flocks passing again under the hands of him that tells them, that is, of the shepherd counting them as they go by, and read it as the sign of settled and ordinary husbandry resumed after a devastation; the counting of a flock presupposes both that there is a flock to count and that there is someone at leisure to count it. Gill lists the same districts without comment, and the passage is generally treated as the concrete filling out of what the previous verse had promised in general terms: the peace is not to be an abstraction or a state of mind, but a matter of animals safely in fields, in named places, under the hand of men whose ordinary work has become possible again.
14:
With the fourteenth verse the promise turns to the Messiah, and the passage that follows is the most contested in the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch set out the structure—the restoration of the monarchy and the priesthood, followed by two supplementary messages guaranteeing the eternal continuance of both—and then report the controversy. The whole portion is wanting in the Greek version, and for that reason, and chiefly because of the promise that not merely the royal house but the Levitical priests should continue for ever and increase innumerably, two scholars have considered it spurious; a third treats several verses as later interpolations and a fourth the whole passage as a series of separate additions made in a later age. Against these, Keil and Delitzsch name four who have shown the reasons worthless and a fifth who has defended the genuineness of the passage, and they quote a sixth who says nothing can be so preposterous and unreasonable as to find later additions here. Adam Clarke approaches the same verse historically, noting that the prophets who predicted the captivity also foretold its conclusion, though not in such express terms as this one; he lists four earlier prophets who spoke of the end of the exile and observes that the Chaldee paraphrase explains these verses of the Messiah. John Gill reads the coming days as future but not remote in God’s reckoning—five or six hundred years and no more—and says the word of attention prefixed marks this as the principal of the great and mighty things God had promised to show the prophet.

John Calvin explains why the promise is set at a distance. God shows here why he had promised a quiet in which no one would take away their flocks by force: the faithful had to look further than their present condition, for they were then exposed to slaughter and, while the unbelieving still entertained vain hopes, the children of God saw a thousand deaths, so that terror almost drove them to despair, and in exile they saw themselves far from their own country without hope of return. The prophet therefore bids them extend their thoughts to a future time, having already fixed the term at seventy years; the favour he predicts could not be laid hold of unless they held their minds in suspense and waited patiently until the appointed time came. On the verb he allows two senses, to raise up and to establish, both of which suit; it sometimes means to rouse, and this way of speaking is fitly used of God’s promises, since they seem for a time to lie dormant before what was hidden is made to appear.

Matthew Henry treats the promise as the crown of all the blessings in the chapter. Christ imparts righteousness to his church, being made of God righteousness to us, and believers are made the righteousness of God in him; his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, though in this world prosperity and adversity succeed one another like day and night. The covenant of priesthood, he says, is secured in the same way, and all true believers are a holy and royal priesthood who offer spiritual sacrifices, themselves first of all as living sacrifices; the promises of that covenant have their full accomplishment in the gospel Israel, since all who walk according to the gospel rule are made the Israel of God, on whom shall be peace and mercy. He ends with a caution against despising the families which were of old the chosen people, though for a time they seem to be cast off. Gill takes the phrase opening the fifteenth verse as marking the very same days already spoken of, the fullness of time agreed between the Father and the Son and fixed by appointment. John Wesley reads the same clause as the appointed season of the promise.
16:
The name given at the sixteenth verse divides the commentators, and the question is grammatical before it is doctrinal. Charles Ellicott observes that while the words reproduce the language of an earlier chapter they do so with a remarkable difference. There the title is given to the future King, and has accordingly been used as a proof of the full divinity of the Christ; here it is given to the city, and so given can only mean that the name will be the motto and watchword of her being. She will be a city marked by a righteousness which is the gift of God; and this, he holds, throws light on the title as applied to the King. Adam Clarke will not allow the received rendering, calling it ignorant and almost impious for making Jerusalem bear the name. The pronoun translated her is the masculine affix in the Chaldaic form, and Blayney renders the clause, And this is He whom Jehovah shall call our righteousness. Clarke offers a sense he thinks nearer the scope of the place—and this one who shall call to her is the Lord our Justification—so that salvation comes when Christ is proclaimed to them as their Justifier. He notes that the Vulgate, the Chaldee and the Syriac read a less ambiguous form, and concludes that this passage and the earlier one were never meant to express the same thing.

John Calvin reads the verse as extending the benefits of the kingdom to the whole people. Without this the promise of a righteous king would have appeared cold, for it sometimes happens that however much a king exercises justice the people continue miserable; the prophet therefore testifies that they would be in every way blessed under the King promised to come. Calvin insists that the salvation meant belongs to the spiritual kingdom: had an earthly government been in view the salvation would have been temporal too, but as the promise concerns a celestial kingdom it must reach to the very heavens, its limits wider than the whole world. John Wesley takes the opposite line, reporting that some understand a spiritual salvation but most and the best interpreters a temporal one, typical of the eternal salvation promised to the true Israel; and he denies flatly that the name is anywhere given to the church. John Gill reads Judah as those who are Jews inwardly, the name signifying one who confesses or praises the Lord, and that the salvation is from sin, from Satan, from the law and from wrath, obtained by the Branch of righteousness, and not withheld from the older dispensation.

At the seventeenth verse Matthew Henry gathers three covenants that seemed broken while the captivity lasted—royalty with David and his seed, priesthood with Aaron and his seed, peculiarity with Abraham and his seed—and promises that all three take place again. The throne was overturned, the crown had fallen, Jeconiah was written childless; but as long as Christ Jesus sits at the right hand of God and is King upon the holy hill of Zion, David does not want a successor and the covenant is not broken. Ellicott adds that the words are hardly more than a repetition of older promises, uttered under very different circumstances: once when the line of David was in all the freshness of its strength, now when it seemed on the very point of dying out. The hope of the prophet is inextinguishable, and he finds an echo of the words at the Annunciation which interprets them. Calvin observes that kingdom and priesthood together secured the safety of the people, for without a king they were a maimed body and without a priest there was nothing but ruin; the two he makes the marks of a true Church. Wesley agrees that the promise relates to Christ, since the line of David had failed long since but for him.
18:
The second half of the promise concerns the priesthood, and every voice reads it as fulfilled otherwise than the words appear to say. John Gill states it bluntly: the Levitical priesthood was abolished long ago, being typical of the priesthood of Christ and succeeded by it, and he is a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, who having offered up himself here on earth now appears in heaven for his people, making intercession; and as long as he continues to do so, which will be always, a man shall not be wanting before the Lord. Charles Ellicott reaches the same end by a fuller road. The promise, he says, received a fulfilment other than the words appeared to imply: the Levitical priesthood passed away, but Christ was made a Priest after the order of Melchizedek, and by virtue of their union with him his people became a holy priesthood, offering not the burnt offerings and meat offerings which were figures of the true, but spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, the sacrifice of body, soul and spirit which alone was acceptable to God. Adam Clarke contributes only a cross reference, treating the clause as a repetition of the promise once made to Phinehas.

Ellicott alone attends to the wording. The combination that names the priests the Levites is not found elsewhere in this prophet, though it appears in five other books; it may indicate either that the priestly character, though not the specific priestly functions, extended to the whole tribe of Levi, or, more probably, that the prophet is speaking of the Levite priests of Judah as contrasted with the priests of the high places, or such as Jeroboam had made of the lowest of the people. He adds that the offering named in the second clause was of meal and frankincense, not of flesh, burnt on the altar so that the fragrant smoke was a sweet savour. John Calvin raises against the priesthood the same difficulty he had raised against the kingdom: the priesthood became corrupted, and for the most part the priests were not only degenerate but altogether sacrilegious, so that the sacerdotal name itself became nothing but a base and wicked profanation of all sacred things.

His answer is that this was the very way God chose to shew that another priest was to be expected, and that men were not to rest in figures but raise their thoughts to him who was to be the only true Mediator. The prophets accommodated their discourses to the men of their own age, and described the kingdom and priesthood of Christ under the external symbols then in use; it is therefore proper to take the ceremonies of the Law as denoting the reality they signified, for Christ offered no calves and no incense, but fulfilled all that the symbols set before the people. Calvin notes that the perfuming of the offering is named though only a small portion of the flour was burnt, a part standing for the whole. John Wesley reads the promise as a ministry to abide in the church to the end of the world, and observes that it is not unusual for God to express promises fulfilled under the gospel by expressions proper to the older covenant. At the nineteenth verse Gill notes that what follows is not a new prophecy but an illustration of the former; and Calvin says the confirmation comes by a similitude: the covenant with the people would be no less firm than the settled order of nature. Unceasing are the progresses of the sun, moon and stars, and continual the succession of day and night: there is rain and then fair weather, and changes in the seasons, but the sun keeps its daily course and the moon is new every month, and this unbroken order declares the wonderful wisdom of God.
20:
The similitude is now turned into a challenge, and John Calvin hears reproof in it: the prophet touches the wickedness of the people, for the Jews did, as far as they could, overthrow the covenant of God by their murmurs; in adversity they instantly thought and said that God had forgotten his covenant. That want of faith is what the challenge answers: why these complaints? It is the same thing as though you sought to pull down the sun and the moon from the heavens, and to subvert the difference between day and night; for I am the same God who settled the succession of day and night and promised that the Church shall continue for ever, and you can no more abolish my covenant with David than the law of nature. Calvin insists this was not said without reproof: they were ungrateful in doubting the truth and constancy of God, and were carried away as by a blind madness when they hesitated to believe his covenant, as though they attempted to subvert the world so that there should be no difference between light and darkness. John Wesley reads the covenant with day and night as the law of God established in the course of natural causes, and draws from it that the gospel ministry in the church, abiding for ever, is as certain as the succession of darkness and light. Adam Clarke offers only a cross reference to an earlier chapter.

John Gill takes David at the twenty-first verse as a type of the Messiah, with whom the covenant of grace is made, which stands fast and will never be broken: as the one is impossible, the hindering of the rotation of day and night, so is the other, the breaking of the covenant concerning the perpetuity of his kingdom. Calvin notes a change of terms: what had been called the throne of the house of Israel is now the throne of David, and he means the same by both, since king and people are relatively connected, and since the posterity of David ruled for the public good and not their own. He observes also that where David had been called the servant of God, the Levites are now called his ministers, a word common in the books of Moses for the Levitical priesthood, meaning to serve.

At the twenty-second verse Calvin finds the particle of comparison left out at the beginning, and identifies the promise as that given to Abraham when he was bidden to look on the heavens and number the stars if he could. That blessing was extended to the whole body of the people; here it is confined to David and to the Levitical tribe, because the safety of the people was grounded on the kingdom and the priesthood. As kings ruled not for themselves, and the sacerdotal dignity had not been given to the Levites for their private advantage but for the people, so the prophet states a part for the whole, and nothing is diminished from the promise, as though the other tribes were not to multiply: what is said of David and of the Levitical tribe extends without difference to the whole Church. Clarke refers the multiplied seed to the spiritual David and his progeny, and argues from history: the two families chosen for the priesthood, that of Aaron and Phinehas, and that of Ithamar after it was taken from him, are both extinct, and the office of priest offering sacrifice has not been exercised for nearly eighteen hundred years, so that the priesthood promised here must be a spiritual one. Wesley reads it the same way, the seed and the Levites multiplied in the multiplying of Christians and of faithful ministers, and Gill contents himself with the figures, the stars of heaven innumerable and the sand of the sea immeasurable.
23:
The chapter closes by answering a saying of the people, and the commentators divide sharply over which two families are meant. Adam Clarke canvasses the options and dismisses two: some think the two kingdoms are meant, but these can never be two distinct families, being of one and the same race; others the families of Jacob and David, but neither were these distinct. If the families that had the priesthood are not meant, then the regal family of David and the sacerdotal family of Jacob through Levi may be designed; and on the spiritual interpretation neither has failed, for Jesus is a King and a Priest, and all true believers in him are kings and priests. John Calvin takes the two families to be the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah, calling it an unhappy event that the people had been divided when they ought to have been one nation, and adding that though the body was torn asunder by the defection of the ten tribes, the election of God was that the seed of Abraham might be one. John Wesley names them the families of David and Aaron, and reads the scorn as a claim that the people should never be a nation more, having rulers of their own and a ministry.

John Gill asks who spoke it, and answers that the question is put to the prophet by interrogation, whether he had considered what he heard the people say. Not the Chaldeans, with whom the prophet was not, but the unbelieving Jews, either the profane part of them, whose view was wicked, to accuse God and discourage the godly, or the weaker sort of the good people, indulging unbelief and despondency. Calvin rejects the same reading: some explain the passage of the Chaldeans, who regarded the people with great contempt, but this is cold and unmeaning, and he has no doubt that God is expostulating with the Israelites, who had relinquished the hope of deliverance. That, he says, is why so much has been repeated: the blessing was regarded as uncertain by the unbelieving, who had so filled their minds with despair that they rejected all his promises and gave no place to faith or hope, and the repetition was not in vain, since it was necessary to contend against their perverse wickedness.

At the twenty-fifth verse Calvin has God oppose the constancy of his own faithfulness to their murmurings, adducing the similitude of nature again: if my constancy is conspicuous in the laws of nature, why do you not ascribe to me my due honour, since I am the same God who created heaven and earth, fixed the laws of nature which remain unchangeable, and made a covenant with my Church? He explains once more why a thing clear in itself is confirmed so often: the contest with the obstinate hopelessness of the people was difficult, for they thought themselves rejected without hope when God was punishing them only for a time. Gill reports at the last verse that a Jewish commentator named Jonah thought Jacob was put in the place of Aaron, because of the two families named before, but objects that in this part of the chapter no mention is made of priests at all; the seed intended is the spiritual seed of Christ, the antitypical David, the Israel of God whether Jews or Gentiles, whom the Lord never casts away. Calvin ends on the promise made to Abraham and repeated to Jacob, joined to the special promise given to David, and on the answer it gives to the objection ready at hand, that the ten tribes were scattered and what remained was not far from ruin. The people were hasty; their expectation ought to have remained in suspense until the time prescribed, and they were to bear their exile patiently, since the salvation promised depended on the gratuitous mercy of God.
